abstract: Fusarium poae is a widespread component of Fusarium head blight (FHB) pathosystems, frequently detected in cereal crops despite limited symptom development during infection. Populations of F. poae comprise closely related lineages with limited evidence of sexual recombination, raising questions about the genomic variation present within this comparatively cryptic pathogen and how it is organized. Here, a genomic analysis of 84 F. poae isolates, including 12 long-read assemblies, was used to characterize population structure and genomic variation within a predominantly contemporary Canadian collection supplemented by isolates from diverse international origins. Long-read assemblies showed that genomes are partitioned into gene-dense core regions and repeat-rich accessory regions (ARs) predicted to encompass entire chromosomes as well as regions near telomeres of core chromosomes. Homologous AR sequences were broadly shared among strains but showed variable organization across the most contiguous assemblies, precluding consistent assignment of discrete accessory chromosome identities. AR-associated loci also exhibited distinct patterns of sequence similarity across distantly related Fusarium species, including unusually high similarity to sequences present in F. langsethiae and F. oxysporum genomes. In addition to genes predicted to be involved in regulation, transport, and metabolism, F. poae ARs encode candidate effectors, secondary metabolite biosynthesis gene clusters, putative antifungal resistance loci, enzymes predicted to be involved in plant host interactions, and an expanded family of hydrophobins. Across long-read assemblies, copy number variation within ARs showed similar locus-specific amplification patterns, consistent with both non-random genome dynamics and shared evolutionary history. Together, these findings support a model of compartmentalized genome evolution in F. poae, in which ARs contribute to genomic plasticity and functional variation in a largely recombination-limited population.
